segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now about food sacrificed to idols: we know that “we all have knowledge.” Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: If anyone thinks they have come to know something, they do not yet know as they ought to know.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But if anyone loves God, that person is known by him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, about eating food sacrificed to idols: we know that “an idol is nothing in the world” and that “there is no God but one.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For even if there are so-called gods, whether in heaven or on earth—as indeed there are many gods and many lords—

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: yet for us there is one God, the Father, from whom all things come and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom all things come and through whom we exist.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But this knowledge is not in everyone. Some, from being used to idols until now, eat this food as food sacrificed to an idol, and their conscience, being weak, is defiled.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But food will not bring us near to God; for we are no better off if we eat, and no worse off if we do not.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But take care that this right of yours does not somehow become a stumbling block to the weak.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For if someone sees you, the one with knowledge, reclining at table in an idol’s temple, will not his conscience, weak as he is, be built up to eat food sacrificed to idols?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the one who is weak is being destroyed by your knowledge—the brother for whom Christ died.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And so, by sinning against your brothers and striking their conscience when it is weak, you sin against Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Therefore, if food causes my brother to fall, I will never eat meat again, so that I may not cause my brother to fall.

notes.note: In a city like Corinth, much of the meat available came from animals offered in temples. Part was burned, part went to the priests, and the rest was eaten at temple meals or sold in the market. The Greek term is a Jewish and Christian one; a pagan would have said simply “sacred offering.” The question put to Paul is whether believers may eat such food.

notes.traditional: we know that we all have knowledge
notes.note: Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks. Most scholars think Paul is here quoting a slogan from the Corinthians' letter to him and then qualifying it. The same is widely held for the two statements quoted in verse 4, and some extend it to verse 8. The words can also be read as Paul's own, which he then limits.

notes.phrase: that person is known by him
notes.traditional: the same is known of him
notes.note: A few early witnesses, including the oldest papyrus copy of Paul's letters, have a shorter text: “if anyone loves, that person is known.” Most manuscripts and most editors have the longer reading translated here. On either reading the point is that being known by God matters more than what one knows.

notes.phrase: “an idol is nothing in the world”
notes.traditional: an idol is nothing in the world
notes.note: The Greek can also be read “there is no idol in the world,” meaning that no idol has real existence. That reading makes a closer parallel with “there is no God but one.” Many recent translations follow it. Either way the claim is that the gods the images represent are not real gods.

The sentence has no verbs in Greek and has the rhythm of a confession. Its wording echoes Israel's daily declaration, “The Lord our God, the Lord is one” (Deuteronomy 6:4). “God” is applied to the Father and “Lord” to Jesus Christ. Many scholars take this as Paul including Jesus within Israel's confession of the one God, though how much to draw from it is debated.

notes.phrase: from being used to idols until now
notes.note: The earliest manuscripts read “custom” or “habit” (synētheia). The later majority reads “conscience” (syneidēsis), which the King James Version follows; it is probably a slip caused by the same word later in the verse. Modern editions and translations follow the earlier reading.

The verb means to present or place someone before another. Here it may mean winning God's favour (“commend”) or, in a courtroom sense, bringing us before God for judgment. In either case the point is that eating or not eating does not affect one's standing with God. Some scholars think this sentence is another Corinthian slogan.

notes.phrase: reclining at table in an idol’s temple
notes.traditional: sit at meat in the idol's temple
notes.note: Temples had dining rooms where people reclined for meals, as was the custom at formal dinners. Such meals marked family occasions, club gatherings and civic events, so declining them carried a social cost. Paul's example is of a believer seen at one of these dinners.

Most translations have “emboldened” or “encouraged.” The Greek verb is the same one used in verse 1, “love builds up.” Paul's repetition is ironic: the knowing person's example “builds up” the weak one into doing what will destroy him. The rendering keeps the echo.

“Brother” was the ordinary term among early believers for a fellow member of the community, and it included women as well as men. The singular is kept here and in verse 13 because Paul is picturing one individual.

The verb ordinarily means to hit or beat someone. “Wounding” is the traditional rendering and describes the result. “Striking” keeps the plain sense of the word: the act is pictured as a blow against a conscience that cannot withstand it.

candidates.reason: Recurs in 1 Corinthians 8–10, Acts 15 and 21, and Revelation 2, where translations vary between “food,” “meat” and “things” and between “sacrificed” and “offered.”
Occurs about thirty times across Paul, Acts, Hebrews and 1 Peter; some scholars argue for “consciousness” or “self-awareness,” so one decision is needed.
Extremely frequent for fellow believers of either sex; the choice between “brother(s)” and “brother(s) and sister(s)” should be made once for the whole New Testament.
Common in the Gospels and Paul, rendered variously as “offend,” “cause to stumble” or “cause to sin,” and needs to be kept distinct from πρόσκομμα (“stumbling block” here).
Varies across the New Testament between “authority,” “right,” “power” and “liberty”; the sense divisions need fixing, especially for 1 Corinthians 8–9.
